dct_description_sm: The purpose of this project is to assess community composition and metabolic potential of freshwater aquatic microbial communities established in several waterbodies throughout the Lake Hazen watershed and how they change over an arctic annual hydrological cycle. Microbes are key energy sources at the base of food chains and are important mediators of several important biogeochemical cycles, such as cycling nitrogen and other nutrients essential for life as well as greenhouse gases, through aquatic ecosystems. Climate change in the North has the effect of increasing glacial melt and permafrost thaw, releasing previously stored nutrients and pollutants into downstream waterbodies, altering resident microbial communities and their roles with unknown consequences.  Because microbial activity can alter water quality, understanding what microbial communities are found in arctic watersheds, how they change over time and the metabolic potential they bring to the region is fundamental to our understanding of how these freshwater ecosystems and the important services they provide may change in the future under different climate change scenarios. From a socio-economic perspective, increasing our ability to predict impacts of warming on arctic freshwater services is vital for securing food, clean drinking water and traditional lifestyles for Northern peoples.
dct_title_s: Characterization of aquatic microbial community composition, community dynamics and metabolic potential of microbes throughout the Lake Hazen watershed
